keep mind occupied all the time

issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts' is inconsistent as written: it is phrased like a trigger ('seeing people...') rather than a strategy the patient uses. Within the Maladaptive Strategies node, the other items are clear coping behaviours, so this item is internally mismatched.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used specifically as a distraction is not impossible, but in this profile it stands out as clinically poorly integrated with the rest of the selected items. The other strategies are avoidance/disengagement (screen use, avoiding people), and the threat/memory profile is hypervigilance plus overwhelm. This item introduces a much more extreme coping style without supporting indicators elsewhere in the five target components, making the strategy set feel internally uneven for the same patient.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a police-related trauma in a 46-year-old civilian graphic designer, self-blame for 'the way I acted' is possible, but here it sits awkwardly beside appraisals that frame the trauma as globally ruining life and draining meaning, without any other items suggesting perceived responsibility, moral failure, or a specific behavior during the event. The appraisal set is therefore less coherent than the other nodes.

vignette:
# Marcus's Case

Marcus Keller was forty-six when he walked into the police station on a Tuesday afternoon in March, ostensibly to report a stolen bicycle. What happened in the next forty minutes would splinter his sense of safety so thoroughly that he would spend the next eighteen months trying to reassemble it in fragments, each piece never quite fitting back together the way it had been before.

The officer who responded to his report had been agitated from the start—responding to a call about a disturbance in the parking lot. Marcus, standing near the entrance with his hands visible and his voice level, had simply been in the wrong place. The officer, already primed for threat, had misread Marcus's posture as evasive. Within seconds, Marcus found himself on the concrete, his arm wrenched behind his back with such force that he heard something pop in his shoulder. His face was pressed against the rough ground. He could taste blood. Another officer arrived and, seeing Marcus on the ground, assumed he was dangerous. What followed was a cascade of escalation—shouting, more hands, the weight of bodies, the sensation of being utterly powerless while people who were supposed to protect him treated him as something to be subdued. When it was over, Marcus had a dislocated shoulder, a lacerated cheek, and a broken rib. The stolen bicycle report was never filed. The incident was ruled a "lawful arrest," though Marcus had committed no crime.

In the weeks after, Marcus returned to his work as a graphic designer at a mid-sized marketing firm, but something had fractured inside him that he could not name. He had always been a calm man, methodical in his approach to design projects, someone his colleagues described as steady. Now his mind would not settle. At his desk, staring at a screen, he would find his thoughts suddenly filled with the sensation of concrete against his face, the smell of the officer's uniform, the helplessness. He would jolt in his chair, his heart racing, and have to excuse himself. The thoughts came without warning, unbidden and vivid, as if his mind had become a space he could no longer control.

He began spending his evenings on his phone, scrolling through games and social media, anything to keep his mind occupied and away from the intrusive images. His wife, Elena, noticed that he would sit beside her on the couch but was not really there. When she tried to talk to him about what had happened, Marcus would start to explain—the force, the unfairness, the way he had done nothing wrong—but the emotion would overwhelm him so completely that he would have to stop. He could not find the words to make her understand. He could not even finish a sentence without feeling as though he were drowning.

Within months, Marcus had begun to avoid situations that felt unpredictable. He stopped going to the grocery store during busy hours, stopped attending his regular Thursday night poker game with friends, stopped going to restaurants where he could not see the exits. Anywhere he went, he would first identify how he could leave quickly, where the doors were, whether there were people in uniform nearby. His body never truly relaxed. Even at home, in the house he had owned for fifteen years, he felt a constant low hum of tension, as if danger were always just outside his peripheral vision.

Elena had begun to withdraw from him, hurt by his distance and frightened by the person he was becoming. His work suffered. He had missed several client meetings, had turned down a promotion that would have required him to attend industry conferences. The meaningful parts of his life—his marriage, his career, the friendships he had cultivated over decades—had all begun to feel hollow, as though trauma had drained them of significance.

What brought Marcus to seek help was a moment of clarity that came with its own despair. He was sitting in his home office, scrolling mindlessly through his phone at two in the morning, unable to sleep, when he realized that he could not remember the last time he had felt present in his own life. The injustice of it—that a man with a badge had destroyed his sense of safety and no one had been held accountable—burned in his chest alongside a deeper terror: that this was who he was now, and that he would never be able to reclaim what he had lost.
